source_notes: NFL.com official standings and Week 8 game results; editorial ranks are 4DK judgments; injury notes reflect reports available 2026-11-03 morning.

teams.name: Buffalo Bills
teams.leaders: Josh Allen: 289 pass yards, 2 pass TD and 1 rush TD vs Baltimore; James Cook: 80 rush yards.
teams.injuries: Josh Palmer exited Week 8 with a hamstring issue; monitor the Week 9 practice report.
analysis: Buffalo has earned the throne. Josh Allen responded to the bye by putting Baltimore under immediate pressure, and the Bills turned what was supposed to be a measuring-stick game into a 36–10 statement. The passing game supplied the explosives, Allen added a rushing score, and the defense took advantage of a Ravens offense forced into emergency quarterback duty. We are not pretending that circumstance did not matter; we are saying Buffalo handled the opportunity like a team that understands its place in the AFC.

The challenge is balance. Buffalo is 6–1, yet its division record is still 0–1 and the defense has allowed 181 points. The Vikings matchup is a genuine test of whether the Bills can dictate terms against a disciplined NFC heavyweight. The offense is already capable of carrying a contender; the next stage is making the rest of the roster equally trustworthy.

teams.name: San Francisco 49ers
teams.week8_result: BYE • last game L 20–29 at Atlanta
teams.leaders: Brock Purdy: 1,748 pass yards, 15 TD, 4 INT and 110.1 passer rating through seven games.
teams.injuries: Offensive health remains a priority after the Atlanta loss; check Week 9 designations before kickoff.
analysis: San Francisco climbs without playing, and that is not a sympathy vote. The 49ers entered the bye at 6–1 with a 58-point differential and a 3–0 division mark. Brock Purdy’s 15 touchdown passes against four interceptions underline how often the offense has operated with purpose. The Atlanta loss remains on the record, but the Week 8 chaos around the league gave us no reason to erase six weeks of strong football.

What we want from the 49ers is a cleaner response to the turnover pressure that Atlanta created. The defense can control a game when its front dictates down and distance, but it cannot keep being asked to repair short fields. The bye offers a chance to reset the offense and address health before a demanding stretch. This is still a serious championship-caliber roster, not a team protected by an old reputation.

teams.name: Denver Broncos
teams.leaders: Jonah Coleman: 41 rush yards, 63 receiving yards and the go-ahead touchdown vs Kansas City.
teams.injuries: Jonah Coleman returned from injury and scored the winner; monitor his workload as it grows.
analysis: Denver is one of the defining stories of this edition. Four straight wins have changed the AFC West from a Kansas City coronation into a real race, and the 28–24 victory over the Chiefs is the clearest proof. The Broncos did not simply survive; they produced the late touchdown they needed and defended the closing sequence with the division on the line. Rookie Jonah Coleman supplied the decisive scoring run and added a receiving dimension that made Denver less predictable.

There is a warning in the numbers: a 6–2 team with only a plus-seven point differential is living in narrow margins. We respect the resilience, but a contender eventually has to put lesser opponents away before the fourth quarter. Bo Nix and the offense are getting the result; we want more consistent early-down efficiency. For now, beating the Chiefs head-to-head earns this climb.

teams.name: Chicago Bears
teams.leaders: Caleb Williams: 24/34, 247 pass yards, 1 TD; D’Andre Swift: 3 rush TD vs Seattle.
teams.injuries: Kyle Monangai was out for MNF (thumb/toe); Caleb Williams has returned from his earlier hamstring absence.
analysis: Chicago went into Seattle on Monday night and left with a 34–17 win that changed our NFC conversation. Caleb Williams was measured rather than reckless, completing 24 of 34 passes for 247 yards, and D’Andre Swift finished three drives with rushing touchdowns. The Bears controlled possession, absorbed Seattle’s push to 20–17, then answered with two touchdowns instead of allowing the crowd to dictate the finish. That is the kind of road performance we want to see from a growing team.

The Bears are 6–2, but the NFC North is unforgiving and an 0–2 division mark still matters. We are raising Chicago because the offense has found structure without losing its creativity. The next step is proving that the physicality and composure travel against Minnesota and Detroit, not merely against opponents outside the division. Caleb has moved from promising to central to the playoff race.

teams.name: Minnesota Vikings
teams.leaders: Kyler Murray: 210 pass yards vs Detroit; Minnesota has allowed 93 points in seven games.
teams.injuries: Theo Jackson exited with a quad issue; Kyler Murray reported late-game hamstring tightness.
analysis: The undefeated run is over. Minnesota’s 19–15 loss at Detroit was not a collapse, but it exposed how thin the margin can be when the offense struggles to finish. The Vikings have allowed only 93 points all season, a remarkable foundation, yet their own 140 points through seven games show why every possession is expensive. The defense keeps them in the fight; the offense must create a little more breathing room.

We are not punishing Minnesota for one close road loss as though six wins disappeared. We are moving them because Buffalo, Denver and Chicago produced stronger Week 8 statements. Kyler Murray’s late hamstring tightness is worth watching, and the Lions are now within striking distance in a stacked NFC North. Minnesota remains elite, but the top of the board demands week-to-week proof.

teams.name: Jacksonville Jaguars
teams.leaders: Trevor Lawrence: 1,690 pass yards, 17 TD, 4 INT; Bhayshul Tuten: 104 rush yards vs Indianapolis.
teams.injuries: Eric Murray (elbow) and DaVon Hamilton (knee) exited Week 8; reassess the short-week availability.
analysis: Jacksonville did exactly what a serious division leader should do to an overmatched opponent: remove the suspense. A 42–7 demolition of Indianapolis, 183 team rushing yards and a defense that has surrendered only 111 points in seven games represent complete football. Trevor Lawrence has 17 touchdown passes and a 112.6 rating, and Bhayshul Tuten’s 104 rushing yards showed that the offense does not need to rely on one script.

The Jaguars have the AFC South in their hands, but the next test arrives fast. Baltimore is injured and reeling, yet desperate teams can become dangerous on short weeks. Jacksonville has to stay disciplined rather than treating the matchup as a formality. The most impressive part of this team is how little help it needs from its opponent: it can win through field position, the run game or Lawrence’s arm.

teams.name: Pittsburgh Steelers
teams.leaders: Jaylen Warren: 143 rush yards vs Cleveland; T.J. Watt: 7.5 season sacks (tied for league lead).
teams.injuries: No new major Week 8 injury confirmed in the reviewed league roundup; recheck Week 9 practice participation.
analysis: Pittsburgh has won four straight, and the 27–6 result against Cleveland was a physical declaration inside a division where nobody gets an easy Sunday. Jaylen Warren rushed for 143 yards and the defense held a Browns offense with capable playmakers to two field goals. T.J. Watt remains tied for the league lead with 7.5 sacks, and the Steelers are turning pressure into control instead of chasing highlight plays.

Our hesitation is not about whether Pittsburgh belongs in the AFC race; it absolutely does. It is about whether the passing offense can take over when a top opponent erases the running lanes. At 6–2, the Steelers lead the AFC North, but Cincinnati is only half a game behind and Cleveland is still close. The identity is real. The ceiling will depend on how much offensive versatility joins it.

teams.name: Kansas City Chiefs
teams.leaders: Patrick Mahomes: 321 pass yards, 3 TD vs Denver; Kenneth Walker III: 770 rush yards and 6 rush TD this season.
teams.injuries: Peter Woods exited with a neck issue; the defensive front needs a Week 9 status check.
analysis: Kansas City has lost two straight, and the 28–24 defeat in Denver hurts because the Chiefs had opportunities to close it. Patrick Mahomes threw for 321 yards and three touchdowns, a reminder that the offense is not suddenly broken after Seattle held it to three points. But the fourth-quarter finish and the inability to keep Denver out of the end zone are meaningful. The Chiefs are 5–2, not in free fall, yet the AFC West no longer belongs to them by default.

Kenneth Walker III has 770 rushing yards and six rushing scores, and that balance still gives Kansas City one of the league’s most dangerous offensive blueprints. The issue is converting strong stretches into complete games. We are not moving Mahomes and company down because of brand fatigue. We are moving them because Denver won the direct argument on the field.

teams.name: Detroit Lions
teams.leaders: Jahmyr Gibbs: 153 rush yards vs Minnesota; 773 rush yards and 8 rush TD in seven games.
teams.injuries: Jack Campbell sustained a neck injury and was hospitalized for monitoring; Brian Branch and D.J. Wonnum had concussions.
analysis: Detroit just handed Minnesota its first loss, and it did it with the kind of hard-nosed execution that defines the NFC North. Jahmyr Gibbs rushed for 153 yards, and the Lions protected a 19–15 advantage when the game demanded discipline. This was not a glossy offensive exhibition; it was proof that Detroit can win when its quarterback does not need to chase 35 points. The Lions are 5–2 with a 2–0 division mark.

The football story comes with a much more important human one. Jack Campbell’s neck injury required hospitalization and monitoring, and we are keeping the focus on his recovery rather than guessing a return date. Detroit also suffered multiple defensive injuries. We can praise the result and still acknowledge that the depth of this defense will be tested. The division race is wide open, but health may determine who survives it.

teams.name: Cincinnati Bengals
teams.leaders: Joe Burrow: 38/48, 462 pass yards, 5 TD, 3 INT vs Tennessee; 20 season pass TD.
teams.injuries: Cashius Howell (wrist) and Cedric Johnson (ankle) were among the Week 8 injuries.
analysis: Joe Burrow put 462 yards and five touchdown passes on Tennessee, then still needed overtime to escape 43–36. That is both the appeal and the concern. Cincinnati has one of the league’s most explosive passing attacks, and Burrow now leads the NFL with 20 passing touchdowns. The Bengals have won three straight and can score in a hurry when their receivers create space.

We cannot ignore three interceptions or a defense that let a one-win opponent score 36 points. The Bengals are too talented to spend every week asking Burrow to rescue the afternoon. At 5–2, they are half a game behind Pittsburgh, and the divisional games ahead will punish that kind of defensive inconsistency. This is a top-ten team because the offense can beat anybody, not because the problems have disappeared.

teams.name: Green Bay Packers
teams.leaders: Jordan Love: 288 pass yards, 3 TD vs Carolina; Christian Watson: 113 receiving yards.
teams.injuries: Sean Rhyan (ankle) and Zaire Franklin (shin) were ruled out before TNF; monitor the next report.
analysis: Green Bay got the Thursday-night work done against Carolina, 27–19, and Jordan Love looked like the quarterback the Packers need. His 288 yards and three touchdowns kept the offense moving, while Christian Watson’s 113 receiving yards stretched the field. The Packers have won four of their last five and have an offense capable of attacking defenses at multiple levels.

The NFC North is so crowded that 5–3 still leaves Green Bay fourth in the division. That is the reality of this conference. The run game and line health need continued attention, and the defense cannot rely on the opponent failing to finish. The Packers are in the wild-card picture today, but their margin for a two-game skid is small. We are buying the offensive improvement while demanding more complete football.

teams.name: New England Patriots
teams.leaders: Rhamondre Stevenson: 82 rush yards vs Miami; Drake Maye: 15 season pass TD.
teams.injuries: No new major Week 8 injury confirmed in the reviewed roundup; monitor official practice reports.
analysis: New England bounced back from the Chicago loss with a 24–19 road win in Miami. That result will not lead the national highlight shows, but winning a divisional road game after a difficult week matters. Drake Maye has 15 touchdown passes on the season, and Rhamondre Stevenson’s 82 rushing yards gave the Patriots a practical counterweight to the passing game.

The Patriots are 5–3 and occupy the AFC’s seventh position in the current standings. They also have a perfect 3–0 division record, a detail that may matter later even though Buffalo leads the East. We still need to see whether New England can consistently finish drives against stronger defenses. This team has earned a meaningful place in the playoff discussion; the next few weeks will show whether it can move beyond the bubble.

teams.name: Cleveland Browns
teams.leaders: Deshaun Watson: 324 pass yards vs Pittsburgh; Harold Fannin Jr.: 154 receiving yards.
teams.injuries: Maliek Collins exited with an elbow issue; monitor the next defensive-line injury report.
analysis: Cleveland went into Pittsburgh and got handled, 27–6. Deshaun Watson threw for 324 yards and Harold Fannin Jr. produced 154 receiving yards, but those numbers did not become touchdowns. That disconnect is the story. Moving the ball between the twenties is not the same as controlling a football game, and the Steelers exposed the difference. The Browns are still 5–3, but the point differential has slipped to minus-34.

We have not forgotten the defense that powered Cleveland’s rise, and one divisional loss does not erase its postseason chances. But this is the kind of game that separates a playoff hopeful from a team with real January leverage. The Browns must improve red-zone efficiency, protect the quarterback and keep the defense from playing exhausted. Pittsburgh made the standard clear.

teams.name: New York Giants
teams.week8_result: BYE • last game W 27–21 at Houston (OT)
teams.leaders: Arvell Reese: 55 tackles, 1.5 sacks and 1 interception in seven games.
teams.injuries: Week 8 bye; fresh Week 9 practice designations are still to come.
analysis: The Giants had their bye at 4–2–1 and remain the NFC East leaders, which is an achievement worth acknowledging in a division where the preseason expectations have been scrambled. The defense has found useful young contributors, including rookie Arvell Reese, and the team has shown it can survive close games without needing a perfect offensive performance.

There is a caution attached to a plus-two point differential: New York is winning on narrow margins. We want to see the offense create more separation and reduce the number of possessions decided by one mistake. The bye was an opportunity to reset before a tougher stretch. The Giants are not a novelty atop the East anymore; they have to start acting like a team capable of keeping that lead.

teams.name: Los Angeles Rams
teams.leaders: Blake Corum: 73 rush yards vs LA Chargers; Rams defense held the Chargers to nine points.
teams.injuries: Cornerbacks Trent McDuffie and Jaylen Watson sustained injuries; Myles Garrett is expected back at practice, not yet confirmed to play.
analysis: The Rams are back to .500 after beating the Chargers 24–9, and the most encouraging development was not a gaudy passing line. It was a defense that forced mistakes and a ground game that kept the opponent from dictating tempo. Blake Corum’s 73 rushing yards helped build a game the Rams could manage rather than chase. Two straight wins have restored some structure to a season that looked unstable.

The ceiling changes if Myles Garrett can return and the cornerback injuries do not hollow out the secondary. Garrett is expected to practice, but we will not turn that into a promised Week 9 appearance. The Rams still trail San Francisco by two and a half games, and their 0–2 division record is a real issue. The path back into the race begins with stacking wins, not talking about pedigree.

teams.name: Seattle Seahawks
teams.leaders: Jaxon Smith-Njigba: 6 catches, 118 yards, 1 TD vs Chicago; 985 season receiving yards.
teams.injuries: Charles Cross (ankle) and Rashid Shaheed (knee) were out Monday; line and receiver depth remain concerns.
analysis: Seattle’s Week 7 demolition of Kansas City was real. So was Monday’s 34–17 loss to Chicago. Both games belong in the evaluation. Jaxon Smith-Njigba delivered another huge night—118 yards and a touchdown—but the offense never established a credible running threat, and Sam Darnold’s interception helped Chicago slam the door. The Seahawks are 4–4 and only 1–3 against the NFC.

That conference record is why we are moving Seattle down sharply. The defense can still make a contender uncomfortable, but the offense cannot ask JSN to win every possession by himself. Charles Cross and Rashid Shaheed were unavailable Monday, and those absences matter to the structure. We believe the ceiling remains higher than the record; now the team has to prove it with a response against Arizona.

teams.name: Tampa Bay Buccaneers
teams.leaders: Bucky Irving: 170 rush yards and a TD vs Atlanta; Tampa Bay defense pitched a shutout.
teams.injuries: YaYa Diaby exited with a knee issue; monitor the Week 9 update.
analysis: A 16–0 shutout of Atlanta may not look explosive, but it was exactly the kind of identity game Tampa Bay needed. Bucky Irving ran for 170 yards and the defense created a nightmare for Michael Penix Jr., turning the Falcons’ passing attack into a series of empty possessions. Tampa has won two straight and is 2–0 in the NFC South.

The Buccaneers are still 3–5, so we are not pretending one shutout repairs the season. But their positive point differential and perfect division mark tell us they are more dangerous than the raw record suggests. The offense must find ways to produce points when the opponent does not hand over short fields. For now, the defense has given Tampa a reason to believe the division remains attainable.

teams.name: Las Vegas Raiders
teams.leaders: Kirk Cousins: 247 pass yards, 3 TD, 0 INT vs NY Jets; Brock Bowers caught a touchdown.
teams.injuries: Darien Porter exited with a groin issue; monitor his practice availability.
analysis: Las Vegas finally stopped a four-game slide, winning 38–33 at the Jets behind three touchdown passes from Kirk Cousins. Brock Bowers supplied another red-zone answer, and the Raiders reminded everyone how quickly this offense can score when the protection holds up. The victory mattered because the season was drifting from a 3–0 opening into something much uglier.

We are moving the Raiders up, but the warning lights remain on. A minus-nine point differential and a defense allowing 230 points through eight games are not contender numbers. The passing game can create the illusion of control while the other side of the ball gives it away. Las Vegas has a chance to reenter the wild-card conversation; that will require a defensive response, not just another shootout.

teams.name: Atlanta Falcons
teams.leaders: Michael Penix Jr.: 125 pass yards and four interceptions vs Tampa Bay; Bijan Robinson: 780 season rush yards.
teams.injuries: Zachariah Branch (hamstring) and Samson Ebukam (hamstring) are ruled out for Week 9.
analysis: One week after ending San Francisco’s unbeaten start, Atlanta failed to score a point in Tampa. That 16–0 shutout is one of the most revealing reversals of the season. Michael Penix Jr. threw four interceptions, and the Falcons could not generate the basic offensive rhythm that made them dangerous against the 49ers. We cannot reward the previous week’s ceiling while ignoring this week’s floor.

Bijan Robinson remains one of the league’s leading rushers with 780 yards, which makes the offensive collapse even more frustrating. The Falcons need a plan that protects Penix from predictable passing situations and makes the run game the foundation rather than a decorative feature. Injuries to Zachariah Branch and Samson Ebukam add another challenge. This team is talented enough to upset a heavyweight, but nowhere near consistent enough to be one.

teams.name: Baltimore Ravens
teams.leaders: Lamar Jackson exited after one play vs Buffalo; Joe Fagnano threw for 91 yards in relief.
teams.injuries: Lamar Jackson needs thumb surgery and is headed to injured reserve; Tyler Huntley also hurt his toe.
analysis: Baltimore’s 36–10 loss to Buffalo is secondary to the devastating quarterback news. Lamar Jackson returned from an ankle absence and injured his throwing-hand thumb on his first offensive snap. Surgery and injured reserve are now part of the outlook, and Tyler Huntley also hurt his toe. A 4–4 team with three straight losses is suddenly facing a crisis at the position that defines its offense.

We are not going to pretend the Ravens can simply replace Lamar’s creation with a different play call. The defense has to shorten games, the running backs must keep the offense out of obvious passing downs, and the coaching staff needs a realistic emergency plan before Thursday against Jacksonville. Baltimore still has a path back, but it is narrower than it was a week ago. The drop reflects both performance and the new uncertainty.

teams.name: Carolina Panthers
teams.leaders: Chuba Hubbard: 81 rush yards vs Green Bay; Bryce Young: 1,921 season pass yards.
teams.injuries: Damien Lewis (knee) and Jaelan Phillips (hamstring) were among the TNF absences.
analysis: Carolina lost 27–19 at Green Bay and has dropped two straight, yet it remains first in the NFC South at 3–4. That contrast explains this division better than any power-ranking debate. Bryce Young has made progress in stretching the field, and Chuba Hubbard supplied 81 rushing yards on Thursday, but the offense still has too many stretches without an answer.

The Panthers are not being asked to look like a 12-win team overnight. They are being asked to take control of a division that is there for the taking. The defense has allowed 193 points in seven games, and the offensive line is managing injuries. Tampa’s defensive resurgence is now a direct threat. Carolina has a division lead on paper; sustaining it will require better finishes and fewer empty drives.

teams.name: Dallas Cowboys
teams.leaders: Dak Prescott: 195 pass yards vs Arizona; CeeDee Lamb: 7 catches, 58 yards.
teams.injuries: Jake Ferguson and Joey Porter Jr. suffered ankle injuries; rookie Caleb Downs sustained a concussion.
analysis: Dallas followed its Monday night breakthrough over Philadelphia by losing 33–30 in overtime to Arizona. The offense produced enough points to win, but the defense could not hold the late lead or close the game in extra time. Dak Prescott threw for 195 yards and CeeDee Lamb caught seven passes, yet the Cowboys were unable to make the decisive possession count. At 3–5, there is no room to hide behind flashes of offensive talent.

The NFC East remains unusually open, but Dallas is two games behind the Giants and cannot keep treating each week as a fresh start. Jake Ferguson, Joey Porter Jr. and Caleb Downs emerged from Sunday with injury concerns, complicating a roster already searching for stability. We are watching whether the Cowboys can finally build a repeatable defensive identity. Without it, even good offensive nights will keep ending in frustration.

teams.name: Washington Commanders
teams.leaders: Jayden Daniels: 217 pass yards vs Philadelphia; Sonny Styles: 52 tackles and 1 sack this season.
teams.injuries: Treylon Burks had a foot issue entering Week 8; recheck Week 9 participation.
analysis: Washington finally has a result to build on. The 27–10 win over Philadelphia ended a stretch in which mistakes kept turning manageable games into losses. Jayden Daniels threw for 217 yards, and the defense held the Eagles scoreless after the first quarter. The Commanders did not need a spectacular offensive night; they needed a complete, disciplined one.

At 2–4–1, Washington remains a long way from the playoff line, and the road record is still winless. But the team has a young defensive centerpiece in Sonny Styles and a quarterback who can stress a defense when the protection is functional. The next task is to stack clean games rather than treating this divisional victory as a season reset. There is still a path to respectability if the execution travels.

teams.name: Houston Texans
teams.week8_result: BYE • last game L 21–27 vs NY Giants (OT)
teams.leaders: Will Anderson Jr.: 7.5 sacks (tied for NFL lead) through Week 8.
teams.injuries: Week 8 bye; monitor the next official injury report rather than assume full availability.
analysis: Houston comes out of its bye at 2–5, and the record is becoming difficult to separate from the underlying football. The Texans have been competitive in stretches, but they have not turned enough of those stretches into wins. Their minus-five point differential suggests they have been closer than the standings show; their 0–4 home record shows why the frustration is justified.

Will Anderson Jr. is tied for the league lead with 7.5 sacks and gives Houston a true defensive game-breaker. The question is whether the offense can stop wasting the field position that kind of defender creates. The bye gave the Texans time to reset protections and situational decisions. We need to see a response immediately, because the AFC South is moving away from them.

teams.name: Arizona Cardinals
teams.leaders: Tyler Allgeier: 147 rush yards, 44 receiving yards and 2 total TD vs Dallas.
teams.injuries: Jeremiyah Love suffered a new ankle injury; Kendrick Bourne has a fractured tibia and is expected to miss extended time.
analysis: Arizona produced one of Week 8’s wildest wins, coming back to beat Dallas 33–30 in overtime. Tyler Allgeier was the force behind it, piling up 147 rushing yards and another 44 receiving yards with two total touchdowns. Gardner Minshew’s three passing scores changed the energy of the offense, and the Cardinals earned the right to celebrate a comeback that looked improbable.

The bigger question is whether this was a one-week spark or the beginning of a new structure. Minshew is set to start Week 9, while Jeremiyah Love has a new ankle injury and Kendrick Bourne faces an extended absence. Arizona has allowed 238 points, the most in the NFC West, so the defense cannot be ignored. We are rewarding the win without mistaking a thrilling finish for a solved season.

teams.name: New Orleans Saints
teams.week8_result: BYE • last game L 10–16 vs Pittsburgh
teams.leaders: Chris Olave: 636 receiving yards through Week 8; Saints had a Week 8 bye.
teams.injuries: Week 8 bye; no new game-day injury data to add.
analysis: New Orleans had the week off at 2–5, but the bye did not change the basic reality: the Saints are chasing a division that is mediocre enough to remain reachable and competitive enough to punish mistakes. Chris Olave has 636 receiving yards, providing a dependable offensive threat even when the team struggles to sustain drives.

The Saints have a 0–4 home record and have lost four of their last five. Those are not numbers that support a major climb. The offense needs better early-down execution and more consistent red-zone finishes, while the defense must stop forcing every game into comeback mode. The opportunity is still there because no NFC South team has separated; New Orleans has to start earning it.

teams.name: New York Jets
teams.leaders: Geno Smith: 290 pass yards; Braelon Allen: 147 rush yards; Adonai Mitchell: 142 receiving yards vs LV.
teams.injuries: Breece Hall was inactive with a quad injury in Week 8; check his next practice status.
analysis: The Jets scored 33 points and still lost to Las Vegas, 38–33. Geno Smith threw for 290 yards, Braelon Allen ran for 147, and Adonai Mitchell added 142 receiving yards. That is enough individual production to win most weeks, which makes the result more concerning. The defense gave up too many explosive plays and could not protect the offense’s work.

At 2–6 and 0–2 in the division, the Jets are losing ground in a conference that has several five-win wild-card candidates. Breece Hall’s quad injury kept him out, but the running game still produced; the real issue is finishing defensively. We are not ignoring the offensive signs of life. We are asking the Jets to turn those yards into a game that the defense can actually close.

teams.name: Miami Dolphins
teams.leaders: Malik Willis: 211 pass yards vs New England; Jacob Rodriguez: 68 tackles this season.
teams.injuries: No new major Week 8 injury confirmed in the reviewed roundup; recheck Week 9 availability.
analysis: Miami’s 24–19 home loss to New England returned the Dolphins to the wrong side of the ledger after their first victory. Malik Willis threw for 211 yards, but the offense could not create enough finishing power against a divisional opponent. At 1–6, the Dolphins are past the point where one encouraging quarter should change the evaluation.

There are useful pieces here, including rookie linebacker Jacob Rodriguez, who has 68 tackles, but the team has allowed 181 points and has yet to win at home. We need to see a coherent identity from week to week. The next step is not a miracle playoff prediction; it is building a football product that can control possession and make opponents work for every point.

teams.name: Philadelphia Eagles
teams.leaders: Philadelphia scored 10 points vs Washington and has lost six straight.
teams.injuries: The offense remains unsettled; confirm quarterback and line availability on the next injury report.
analysis: Six consecutive losses. That is the number defining Philadelphia after a 27–10 defeat at Washington. The Eagles scored ten first-quarter points and then disappeared offensively, while the defense watched a division rival take over the second half. A roster with this much recognizable talent cannot keep treating each collapse as an isolated accident.

The Eagles are 2–6 and have lost all five of their most recent games. The NFC East is not out of reach mathematically, but the current trajectory is not credible playoff football. Philadelphia needs stability at quarterback, cleaner protection and a defensive plan that can survive when the offense stalls. We are keeping them near the bottom because the body of work demands it, not because we expect the talent to stay quiet forever.

teams.name: Tennessee Titans
teams.leaders: Cam Ward: 304 pass yards, 2 TD, 0 INT; Tony Pollard: 117 rush yards vs Cincinnati.
teams.injuries: Calvin Ridley was active after a hip designation; monitor his status ahead of Week 9.
analysis: Tennessee lost 43–36 in overtime at Cincinnati, but the performance was not empty. Cam Ward threw for 304 yards with two touchdowns and no interceptions, and Tony Pollard rushed for 117 yards. The Titans forced a talented Bengals team into a full-game fight, and the offense showed more life than the 1–7 record suggests.

The reason they are still near the bottom is straightforward: good offensive afternoons do not count as wins, and the defense could not finish. Tennessee has allowed 199 points through eight games. Carnell Tate’s development and Ward’s composure are meaningful building blocks, but the organization needs to convert those flashes into sustained execution. We are watching for growth, not manufacturing a turnaround that has not arrived.

teams.name: Indianapolis Colts
teams.leaders: Indianapolis was outscored 42–7 by Jacksonville; the Colts have dropped four straight.
teams.injuries: No new major Week 8 injury confirmed in the reviewed roundup; assess the response after a heavy defeat.
analysis: Indianapolis was beaten 42–7 by Jacksonville, and there is no respectable way to soften that score. The Colts have lost four straight, have a minus-61 point differential and were overwhelmed by a division opponent that looked faster and more organized in every phase. This is not a one-week overreaction; it is the accumulation of problems the team has failed to solve.

The Colts need a reset in protection, defensive tackling and situational football. The offense cannot spend entire halves without generating a credible scoring threat, and the defense cannot surrender explosive drives without forcing an answer. There are still enough games to change the season’s direction, but the first goal has to be competence from snap to snap. The ranking reflects the current product.

teams.name: Los Angeles Chargers
teams.leaders: Justin Herbert: 257 pass yards, 0 TD, 2 INT vs LA Rams; Chargers are 0–7.
teams.injuries: Daiyan Henley suffered a shoulder injury in Week 8; monitor the next report.
analysis: The Chargers are 0–7 after a 24–9 loss to the Rams. Justin Herbert threw for 257 yards but was intercepted twice, and the offense once again failed to turn possession into points. Los Angeles has scored only 99 points in seven games, the lowest total in the AFC. The record is not a statistical fluke; it is a direct reflection of an offense that cannot consistently finish.

We still believe Herbert has the talent to elevate a team, but one quarterback cannot repair protection, rushing efficiency and defensive mistakes alone. The Chargers have to focus on ending the losing streak and building something repeatable before talking about a larger turnaround. They remain No. 32 because there is no defensible argument for moving a winless team above opponents that are finding ways to finish games.

mvp.name: Josh Allen
mvp.stats: 1,793 pass yds · 11 pass TD · 5 INT · 270 rush yds · 9 rush TD
mvp.analysis: The throne remains his because no contender depends on one player in quite the same way. Allen threw for 289 yards and two touchdowns against Baltimore and added a rushing score. Buffalo is 6–1, and his ability to force defenses to account for both the vertical pass and the quarterback run is the engine of that record. The Bills have imperfections, but Allen keeps turning them into manageable problems. We need a challenger to match his complete influence, not merely his passing total.

mvp.name: Jared Goff
mvp.analysis: Goff climbs because his season has been remarkably efficient and Detroit has just beaten unbeaten Minnesota. Fifteen touchdowns against one interception through seven games is elite control of the football. Gibbs carried the ground game against the Vikings, and that is part of Goff’s case rather than a reason to dismiss him: the quarterback keeps the offense balanced, organized and difficult to predict. The Lions have a genuine two-star engine, but Goff remains its conductor.

mvp.name: Brock Purdy
mvp.analysis: Purdy held steady through the bye because the full body of work still demands respect. Fifteen touchdown passes, a 110.1 rating and a 6–1 record are not accidents. The Atlanta loss revealed what happens when the offense loses the turnover battle, so the response matters more than the week off. We are looking for him to control the game when his first read is taken away and the easy throws disappear. He remains close to the top because he has already done it consistently.

mvp.name: Jaxon Smith-Njigba
mvp.analysis: The team lost, but JSN did not disappear. Six catches, 118 yards and a touchdown against Chicago pushed him to 985 yards and nine scores in eight games. That is outrageous production for a player every defense knows it must stop. We are not giving him an automatic quarterback-style MVP advantage, but we are refusing to erase his value because Seattle is 4–4. The Seahawks’ offense becomes dangerously one-dimensional without him. His individual case is stronger than the team record.

mvp.name: Joe Burrow
mvp.stats: 2,115 pass yds · NFL-best 20 pass TD · 6 INT · 111.6 rating
mvp.analysis: Burrow crashes the top five after a 462-yard, five-touchdown performance against Tennessee. He now leads the league with 20 passing touchdowns and is driving Cincinnati’s three-game winning streak. The three interceptions matter, and needing overtime against a one-win opponent is a fair criticism of the team. But an MVP discussion has to account for the quarterback who repeatedly rescues games with high-level creation. If the Bengals defense stabilizes, Burrow has the numbers to challenge the top three.

mvp.name: Trevor Lawrence
mvp.analysis: Lawrence is playing the cleanest football of his career, and Jacksonville’s 42–7 demolition of Indianapolis gave him another statement result. His 112.6 rating is among the league’s best, and 17 touchdown passes in seven games explain why the Jaguars are running away from the AFC South. We are not ranking him purely on one blowout; we are rewarding an offense that can attack through him without becoming entirely dependent on his arm. A tougher opponent will test whether this level holds.

mvp.name: Kenneth Walker III
mvp.stats: 770 rush yds · 6 rush TD · 131 receiving yds · 2 receiving TD
mvp.analysis: Walker slides because Kansas City has lost two straight and his Week 8 rushing output was 69 yards. But 770 rushing yards through seven games still places him among the league’s leaders, and eight total touchdowns explain how much he changed the Chiefs’ offensive structure. We do not remove a running back from serious consideration because two defenses made him work. We do ask him to dominate the next marquee game, especially with the AFC West now controlled by Denver.

mvp.name: Caleb Williams
mvp.stats: 1,267 pass yds · 6 pass TD · 1 INT in 5 games · 104.6 rating
mvp.analysis: Caleb keeps his place after a composed Monday night road win. He completed 24 of 34 throws for 247 yards and a touchdown, then let D’Andre Swift finish drives on the ground. That is quarterbacking, not a lack of ambition. Chicago is 6–2, and Williams has played only five games after a hamstring absence, so the cumulative totals are lower than some rivals. His command of the offense and ability to avoid mistakes make the argument. He can climb if the Bears keep winning.

mvp.name: Jahmyr Gibbs
mvp.stats: 773 rush yds · 8 rush TD · 285 receiving yds · 2 receiving TD
mvp.analysis: Gibbs earns the promotion after 153 rushing yards against Minnesota. He has more than 1,000 yards from scrimmage and ten total touchdowns in seven games, production that forces every defensive coordinator to adjust the front and coverage shell. We do not view him as a sidekick to Goff. He is the explosive element that makes Detroit’s offense so hard to defend. The MVP hill is steep for a running back sharing credit with an efficient quarterback, but his weekly impact belongs on this board.

mvp.name: Patrick Mahomes
mvp.analysis: Mahomes stays in the ten because the Denver loss was not an individual collapse: he threw for 321 yards and three touchdowns. But we are not handing out reputation votes. Kansas City has lost two straight, and the quarterback of a five-win team cannot stay ahead of players driving stronger current momentum without better finishes. Mahomes has the ability to climb this list faster than almost anyone. The next statement must come in the win column.

rookies.name: Sonny Styles
rookies.analysis: Styles keeps the top spot because the Commanders are asking him to handle real defensive responsibility, and he keeps answering. Washington beat Philadelphia 27–10, and his presence in the middle helps explain why the defense can close throwing lanes without abandoning the run. He is not just a tackle collector; he reads blocking surfaces, covers space and changes what offenses are willing to attempt. Bailey has the louder pass-rush résumé, but Styles still gives us the broader every-down impact.

rookies.name: David Bailey
rookies.analysis: Bailey remains close enough to take No. 1 with one dominant afternoon. Five and a half sacks are not a projection; they are production that changes protection calls. The Jets have struggled to finish games, but that should not bury the rookie defender most capable of disrupting a third-down plan by himself. We want to see him convert more of that pressure into game-turning stops. He stays second because Styles is influencing more phases, not because Bailey has cooled off.

rookies.name: Arvell Reese
rookies.analysis: Reese moves into the top three after the Giants’ bye because the sustained body of work has become too substantial to overlook. He has 55 tackles, a sack and a half and an interception in seven games, with a role that requires him to recognize runs and survive in coverage. This is the difference between a gifted athlete and a dependable NFL defender. The next leap is making more of those tackles behind the line, but the foundation is already worthy of a top-three spot.

rookies.name: Denzel Boston
rookies.analysis: Boston climbs even after Cleveland’s ugly loss because his season production is stronger than the previous board fully captured. Twenty-six receptions for 409 yards and three touchdowns give the Browns a vertical and contested-catch threat that the offense desperately needs. He is not responsible for the failure to convert 324 passing yards into touchdowns against Pittsburgh. The challenge is turning individual flashes into weekly command of coverage. His ability to win downfield has earned this promotion.

rookies.name: Jacob Rodriguez
rookies.analysis: Rodriguez holds the top five because his workload has become impossible to dismiss. Sixty-eight tackles in seven games reflect a defender who diagnoses quickly and stays involved across formations. Miami’s record is poor, but that does not reduce the difficulty of what he is being asked to do. We want to see more third-down and turnover impact as the season continues. For now, the instincts and reliability are a legitimate foundation for a rookie-of-the-year case.

rookies.name: Carnell Tate
rookies.analysis: Tate drops three spots because the defensive rookies and Boston have supplied stronger recent arguments, not because his season has been disappointing. Thirty-four catches and 413 yards on a one-win offense remain impressive. Cam Ward’s 304-yard afternoon against Cincinnati showed the passing game can grow, and Tate remains an important part of that future. The next stage is finishing more drives and turning target share into scores. We are keeping the standard high because the ceiling is high.

rookies.name: Mansoor Delane
rookies.analysis: Delane stays seventh because coverage responsibility matters even when it does not produce a highlight. The Chiefs have trusted him with meaningful snaps, and an interception plus five passes defended in five appearances gives us a tangible baseline. Denver exposed problems in Kansas City’s ability to finish defensively, so the young corner has to help stabilize the back end. We are watching technique, leverage and third-down discipline as closely as the box score.

rookies.name: Germie Bernard
rookies.analysis: Bernard climbs two places because he is becoming a reliable piece of a winning offense. Thirty-two receptions in eight games represent consistent involvement, and his ability to create underneath options matters when Pittsburgh builds its identity around the run and defense. He is not yet the most explosive rookie receiver, but the weekly role is real. The next step is stretching the field and producing more scoring plays without losing the trust he has earned.

rookies.name: Jonah Coleman
rookies.stats: 134 rush yds · 2 rush TD · 97 receiving yds (4 games)
rookies.analysis: Coleman is our new entry because his best work arrived in the biggest moment. Against Kansas City he supplied 41 rushing yards, 63 receiving yards and the late touchdown that put Denver in front. His season totals are still modest after an injury interruption, so we are not inventing a full-season résumé. We are rewarding a rookie who returned, handled meaningful touches and helped decide a division game. Sustaining that role will determine whether he stays.

rookies.name: Jeremiyah Love
rookies.stats: 268 rush yds · 1 rush TD · 36 receiving yds · 1 receiving TD
rookies.analysis: Love remains in the ten, but the new ankle injury clouds the immediate outlook. He has 268 rushing yards in six games and has flashed enough acceleration to matter when Arizona gets him space. Tyler Allgeier carried the comeback against Dallas after Love exited, which illustrates both the roster depth and the rookie’s need to get healthy. We will not guess at a return date. His talent keeps him here; availability and consistent efficiency will decide whether he can climb.
